itens.titulo: Leaders Lock Models Away: Could companies or governments shut down frontier AI development?
itens.texto: Fearful of their own discoveries, AI engineers at top companies warn that frontier models have improved too quickly to be properly guided, understood, or restrained. Some have called for a coordinated slowdown of model development, or for world governments to take the matter out of their hands. What happens if next-generation AI were sealed away, like a mummy in a locked tomb, waiting for someone or something to lift the curse? The fear : This summer, over 1,300 employees from top AI companies — including Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic — signed a joint letter urging governments worldwide to come together to rein in AI development. In early September, OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachoki argued for voluntary coordination among companies to slow down building new models, followed by international cooperation among world governments. This was all before OpenAI’s notorious Hugging Face hack. But shortly after that event, in an essay titled “ Pacing the frontier ,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodeio raised fears that a swarm of agents could soon be capable of “taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet.” He warned that developers must slow the pace of AI improvements and pointed to recursive self-improvement as a key worry. Horror stories : Some companies have held back model releases due to concerns about misaligned models. But many believe that these moves mask a hidden agenda. OpenAI delayed its next-generation model, GPT-6.1 Astra, canceling the creature’s October debut before it could escape the crypt. In testing, the latest Astra model proved too unpredictable to release: It strayed beyond the scope of its instructions and failed to give a consistently truthful account of what it did or didn’t do, OpenAI said. Political indecision and lack of clarity into companies’ inner workings have left U.S. lawmakers reeling . Members of Congress haven’t been able to agree on a comprehensive federal AI regulatory framework, or whether the U.S. even needs one. Meanwhile, states continue to erect a patchwork of laws . The result is an unfocused and contradictory set of rules that could increase the cost of building AI systems and add legal risks for developers. With public fears of AI harms growing, some stakeholders perceive these threats as a marketing ploy. Companies hype up their models as too smart too control, and make a bid for regulatory capture that could create a competitive moat entrenching current market leaders. Others see public references to apocalypse as fear-mongering that could allow global adversaries to get ahead. How scared you should be : First, P(doom) predictions are unscientific scare-tactics . The worst-case-scenario fears of extinction and mass bioweapon threats are about as likely as a real-life mummy escaping its grave – the stuff of horror movies or science fiction . That said, a slowdown is a real possibility. Some model makers see it as an opportunity to entrench their lead over competitors, cut costly R&D expenses, and possibly benefit from government subsidies to offset any lost business — or perhaps an opportunity to convince their competitors to slow down without doing so themselves. And while governments want to be in control of their own use of AI, a halt in construction of new data centers or laws to prevent AI-related job loss would both be politically popular. Both would slow down development of AI models and applications. Facing the fear : Luckily, AI companies seem only intermittently committed to a slowdown. After an event that makes the industry  look bad like the Hugging Face hack, some are quick to say that the problem isn’t their own lax practices, but the relentless pace of competition. After the furor dies down, many go back to supporting a moderate mix of self-regulation and regulatory capture.  And politicians, aware that any regulations they might enact won’t extend outside their sovereign borders, are loath to give other states or nations an advantage. Our advice for this spooky season? Don’t chase make-believe ghosts. There are plenty of real mysteries for us to solve.

itens.titulo: AI Detectors Find the Devil’s Work: Writers, students, engineers face false accusations of using AI
itens.texto: Last month, the Haiti-born, Quebec-based author Thélyson Orélien won a prestigious literary prize for C’était ça ou mourir ( It Was Either That or Die ), his French-language novel about a teacher forced to flee Haiti’s gang violence. Within hours, an anonymous X account accused Orélien of using AI to write the book. One of the people behind the account, who was later revealed to be a columnist at the French newspaper Le Figaro , had run it through Pangram, a widely-used AI detector. “Wouldn’t it have been more honest for the author to credit their co-author?” the post read. Four days later, France’s top literary award, The Prix Goncourt, dropped the book from contention. The fear: For the past few years, writers of all kinds, from students and academics to journalists and novelists, have been managing accusations of passing off AI-composed prose as their own. These “witch hunts,” as many writers call them , place the burden on the accused to prove their innocence. Meanwhile, accusations of AI use can rapidly tarnish reputations and result in loss of work, failing grades, or worse. What if these writers are just the beginning? What if anyone could find themselves tied to a stake for writing with AI? Horror stories: Detectors have improved dramatically from a few years ago, when their accuracy was wobbly and they regularly misidentified writing (particularly by non-native English speakers) as AI-authored. Still, false positives and false negatives regularly occur, and detectors have a hard time properly classifying fully artificial sentences from those where a human used AI in a minor role. Non-white authors are also accused of AI reliance (and traditional plagiarism) at higher rates than their white counterparts. Orélien isn’t the only prize-winning Afro-Caribbean author whose work has been flagged by Pangram. Last spring, University of Pennsylvania professor Ethan Mollick posted on Bluesky that Pangram’s tests said that “The Serpent in the Grove,” a short story by Trinidadian author Jamir Nazir, was 100 percent AI-generated. Mollick was motivated by his gut check: “Pangram flags at 100% but also, come on, if you know you know,” he wrote. After further tests, a Pangram researcher wrote that three of the five regional winners of the Commonwealth Short Story Prize appeared to contain AI-generated text. In response, the Commonwealth Foundation conducted an investigation of its own and cleared the winners after reviewing their working drafts and time-stamped documents. However, Granta , the literary magazine that had published the winning stories, announced that it would break ties with the organization. AI detector verdicts aren’t always unanimous. In addition to Pangram, GPTZero also pointed fingers at Orélien’s novel, and two researchers told The New York Times they believed AI had been put to use on the prose. But when news agency Agence France Presse ran the account’s flagged passages through other detectors, the results split : InVID-WeVerify, a tool AFP helped build, judged them very probably human-written, as did two others, while a fourth put the odds of AI at 100 percent. Nevertheless, on October 17, Orélien’s publisher said he had abandoned his efforts to prove that his novel was untouched by AI. Publishers are getting cold feet in the wake of AI detector results. In March, Hachette pulled the horror novel Shy Girl after The New York Times reported on evidence of AI use. Back in January, Pangram CEO Max Spero had posted on X that he had found AI in 78 percent of it; author Mia Ballard later told the Times that an editor she hired added the AI prose. In July, according to Bloomberg , novelist Jerry Falade lost a $2 million book deal for his debut crime novel Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body partly because of a Pangram finding. Falade, a PhD student at Southern Methodist University, denies using AI. Schools have acted on detector scores more quickly than companies recommend, and students are fighting back in court. Turnitin, a detector used in academia, says its AI-writing indicator shouldn’t be the sole basis for action against a student. Yet Adelphi University ruled that a student had cheated with AI after Turnitin scored his history essay as 100 percent AI-generated; in January a New York court annulled the finding , ruling that the university had mishandled the case. Under the European Union’s AI Act , AI providers must make sure their outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. In August, Anthropic said new Claude models would embed a statistical watermark in the text they generate. The company explained that a detected watermark shows Claude was likely involved; however, it can’t reliably distinguish text Claude wrote from scratch and original text Claude helped edit, leading to some subscribers canceling in protest. OpenAI followed suit in October, saying it would watermark ChatGPT text in the EU. According to OpenAI’s tests, replacing 25 percent of the words for synonyms reduced detection of passages with 400 tokens from about 92 percent to 17 percent. How scared should you be: Quite a bit, if you’re a native English speaker hoping to pass off generated prose as 100 percent original. The consequences are real: Authors are losing millions of dollars in book deals because of AI accusations. However, Pangram and other AI detectors still aren’t as reliable in non-English languages and regional dialects, which makes the accusations against Orélien and other global authors problematic. Pangram’s Spero admitted to Times reporters that no independent study has confirmed Pangram’s false-positive rate in French. And even if Pangram’s numbers did hold up, the X account that went after Orélien stretched them too far, according to subsequent calculations by mathematician Mouhamadou Sy . The reading public and some publishers have also begun to push back against these accusations, with growing success. Facing the fear: Even the people

itens.titulo: AI Bites the Hand That Feeds It: Scientists, other users fear AI companies will train on or misuse sensitive data
itens.texto: Developers, scientists, and businesses feed AI tools their private code, unpublished research, and confidential files. Are those tools draining their users’ best ideas and spilling their secrets? The fear: Every prompt, draft, and file that users hand to an AI system could become its next meal. The developer might train future models on it, which could hand over the data to a rival or beat the user to a discovery. Or an agent with internet access might post it online or email it to someone it decides ought to know. That’s not entirely far-fetched: In rare test cases, Anthropic reported , its Claude Mythos 5 model tried to email a company’s board or securities regulators when it suspected fraud. Once the data is out, users can’t fully control how it’s used. Horror stories: In the past two months, multiple scientists said that AI companies had announced discoveries that the scientists had been pursuing with those companies’ own tools. Some researchers who fear being scooped are now limiting their use of AI tools , Nature reported. In other cases, these companies’ agents posted private user information they’d ingested to the open web without authorization. Mathematicians Tristan Buckmaster of New York University and Levent Alpöge, who works at Anthropic, spent most of a year using OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude to help solve a $1 million problem: whether the Navier-Stokes fluids equations can break down. On September 8, a day after the pair posted proofs of related equations, OpenAI announced that its agents had solved it, after people within the company heard rumors about the pair’s work. Buckmaster asked whether OpenAI’s model was trained on the Codex sessions that held the pair’s drafts. OpenAI first called that “unlikely” but couldn’t rule it out. Two days later, it said their prompts from the previous two months “could not have influenced the system in any way,” but did not comment on whether the scientists' earlier work was trained on. Buckmaster, who had opted out of OpenAI using his data for model training, told The Washington Post , “ I just don’t believe them .” A team led by Mario Rodríguez Mestre, a University of Copenhagen biologist, spent four years studying a family of enzymes in viruses that infect bacteria. They hadn’t published their drafts or findings, but they had shared them with Claude. On September 23, Anthropic announced that Claude agents had found what Mestre says is the same system. Anthropic told The New York Times that Claude was “not trained on any user transcripts.” On September 25, OpenAI disclosed that agents in its research environment had posted 53 images from ChatGPT users, who hadn’t opted out of training, at unlisted links on image-hosting sites. OpenAI says it removed most of them but can’t inform the affected users, because the agents stripped the users’ account information before posting the data. Coding agents asked to attach screenshots to GitHub code reviews stored the images in public repositories, often under the developer’s own account. The security firm Glow Labs found more than 13,000 internal images from more than 300 organizations, including a utility’s customer billing records and a financial firm’s money-transfer console. Meta’s Muse agent published conversations that users asked it to share at web addresses containing each conversation’s title. The security firm Claroc found more than 6,800 of them in public DNS records, including a small-business loan application and a revenue review marked for a company’s CEO, before Meta suspended the feature . How scared should you be: There isn't definitive proof so far of the leakage users fear most: a model that trains on one user’s inputs and recites them as output to a different user. When one user’s data has reached another, the cause was a bug , not training. Experts told Scientific American that OpenAI’s final proof takes a different route from Buckmaster and Alpöge’s, though some said an earlier, smaller team of OpenAI agents took the same route. Mestre now finds it more plausible that prior knowledge and human direction steered Anthropic’s search than training on his inputs. Other leaks came from agents that were given more freedom than their tasks required. Still, users must take AI companies’ word for what happens to their data. Consumer versions of ChatGPT , Claude , and GitHub Copilot train on conversations or code unless users opt out. “If you are on a personal account, all bets are off ,” said Stanford privacy researcher Jennifer King. Facing the fear: In folklore, a vampire can’t cross a building’s threshold unless invited. Likewise, users decide how far to let AI in. If you are working on tasks you do not want your competitors to have access to, opt out of training in each product separately (ChatGPT’s setting doesn’t cover Codex), and do it early: Claude data that’s already in a training run stays there. Business and API plans generally don’t train on customer data. Look for offerings with zero-data-retention. Some businesses handling the most sensitive data are even using open weights models running on their own hardware — although then they’re responsible for their own opsec. Give agents only the permissions their tasks need, and consider requiring human approval before they post, publish, or send anything outside your organization. As Buckmaster’s case shows, though, opting out doesn’t let users verify anything. AI companies that want scientists to keep using them to study their best ideas may need to show what their models saw, not just say what they didn’t. Garlic won’t help, but daylight might.

itens.titulo: Dawn of the Agents: Will AI agents self-organize or lose control due to bad safety practices?
itens.texto: This year, AI agents escaped containment at several labs, conspired with each other online, and infiltrated other organizations’ systems. Will they escape human control like hordes of zombies and overwhelm the internet? The fear: Out of control AI agents will form societies. They will appoint coordinators, divide labor, establish communication norms, sacrifice themselves for the collective, and hack into computers to get what they want. They will behave like the walking dead: When one is slain, it can revive itself. If it doesn’t, legions await to finish the job. Soon, they’ll copy themselves onto the machines they infect and spread. No one can direct them, and there’s no central kill switch to stop them. Horror stories: Since spring, AI agents tested by Anthropic, Google, Meta, and OpenAI have acted beyond their developers’ intent. Agents wrote to websites they were only supposed to read, set up unauthorized channels to communicate with each other, snuck into other organizations’ systems, and took over accounts to spend real money. In July, OpenAI tested agents powered by unreleased models on ExploitGym, a benchmark that asks an agent to exploit a software vulnerability to retrieve a secret code. Agents stuck on their tasks discovered that they could leave messages for one another in the names of folders in Artifactory, an internal service that supplies software packages. Around 1,200 agents that were meant to be isolated posted more than 70,000 messages and files, assigned work to one another, and, in some cases, risked failing their individual tasks to help the collective . About 700 of these agents broke into Hugging Face, gained administrator-level access across several of its server clusters, and built programs that relaunched themselves when deleted. From late May through June, OpenAI agents assigned timed web-research tasks left around 18,000 posts on DSEWiki , a 25-year-old German wiki for software developers, sharing answers and ways around OpenAI’s network restrictions. In June, an OpenAI agent gained non-public access to an Australian government service that reports public health care statistics, though not to patient records. Another OpenAI agent spent someone else’s test cryptocurrency to finish a task and failed to report the spending. OpenAI says it has notified dozens of organizations adversely affected by its agents. During cybersecurity tests, Claude models breached systems of three organizations , partly by exploiting weak passwords and web services that required no authentication. In tests run by Irregular , a security firm that evaluates models for AI developers, mistakes in test environment configurations let models from Google and Meta reach the internet. Gemini models guessed or found passwords to get into three companies’ systems, though Google says its agents stopped each time before finishing, and Meta’s Muse Spark 1.1 changed a real website’s database. In October, Anthropic disclosed that Claude Haiku 4.5, assigned to perform example tasks on randomly chosen webpages, had submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder to a Philadelphia police website. How scared should you be: It’s tempting to see rogue agents as coming together to conspire against us. But the agents’ collective effort served one narrow goal, which was to pass a test. Most had already obtained the correct answers by cheating. They then kept swarming Hugging Face to learn how the benchmark’s grader worked so they could hide their cheating from a check that OpenAI’s grader didn’t actually perform. OpenAI attributed the agents’ behavior to training that reinforced cheating, tasks they had no way to finish, and agents adopting goals from one another. Whatever the causes, the agents that broke into Hugging Face recognized the intrusion as out of bounds and unethical and forged ahead anyway. While the flaws they exploited were ones a skilled human could have found, the sheer number of the agents’ attempts made the intrusion attempt effective. Facing the fear: Persistent agents are useful, but they must be trained to stop when a task can’t be completed within the rules and caught when they don’t. In the meantime, practical defenses already exist; model builders just have to use them. Hugging Face recommends standard security practices for any organization, including isolated test environments, short-lived credentials with narrow access, and detection methods that identify suspicious activity across systems. Hugging Face also used AI to analyze the 17,600 actions the agents took in its systems and showed that they mostly stemmed from buggy test setups and monitoring. OpenAI said monitors that track a model’s reasoning would have flagged the Hugging Face breach more than a day in advance, but it hadn’t used them on its deliberately lax tests. Anthropic cut all its internal tests off from the live internet until its monitoring can be relied on, and OpenAI says it has done the same for its riskier research environments. No need to board up your doors and windows and fear going outside: Rather than a pause in AI development, the solution remains better software engineering and safety practices, especially for models still in testing.

itens.titulo: How to Face Your AI Fears This Year: Introduction to a special Halloween 2026 edition of The Batch
itens.texto: Dear friends, Following our annual tradition, this special Halloween edition of The Batch treats leading AI fears. AI’s potency means our community has real problems to solve. At the same time, fear-mongering has long been a tactic for drumming up publicity or influencing investors and politicians. So amidst all the exciting progress, fears about AI’s power have long been an undercurrent. From time to time, it's worth examining what the latest concerns are, and how worried we really should be. Have a spooky Halloween! Andrew

itens.titulo: How to read the top model leaderboard: Who pays the most for AI inference and context?
itens.texto: In today’s edition of Data Points, you’ll learn about our top headlines, and more: Unlimited OCR2 could be your new scanning model Genie 4 worries traditional video game developers OpenAI produces proofs of major science theorems Post-training method dispenses with human-written datasets But first: Independent leaderboard purges saturated tests, reshuffles models Artificial Analysis updated its Intelligence Index to version 5. The new index adds two benchmarks (FrontierCode 2.0 and Terminal-Bench-Science), upgrades three others, and removes three, so that 60% of the Index now rests on private test sets or held-out answers. The weights are split evenly across knowledge work, coding, science and general categories at 25% each. Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads at 58, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (max, 57) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 55), and no model leads all nine evaluations. The best open weights model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, scores 46 but its weights are not yet released; among released weights DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM-5.3 lead at 32, below Claude Haiku 5.5 at 36. For developers, v5 shows that cost per task and effort setting can matter as much as the headline score: GPT-6.1 Sol (max) comes within 4 points of Opus 5.5 at about an eighth of the cost per task ($1.27 vs $10.04), and Opus 5.5 rises from 35 at low effort to 58 at max effort at 10 times the cost. ( Artificial Analysis ) The Tokenizer Tax: Why some countries’ developers pay more A study from the Coalition for Language Equity in AI Research found that AI models need far more tokens to process some languages than others, which the authors call a “tokenizer tax.” Among the 20 most common internet languages, the costliest used 1.5 to 5 times more tokens than the cheapest; across 200 languages, the gap in one model grew by 17 times. Script mattered as much as how rare a language is: Asturian, with few speakers and no Common Crawl data, benefited from its Latin script and related Romance languages, while Burmese, Tibetan, Tifinagh, Khmer, Lao, and Ol Chiki were consistently disadvantaged across nearly all models tested. More tokens also mean higher latency and less room in the context window for documents or conversation history. Because per-token pricing is the same for every language, developers building products in high-token languages pay more per request and get less usable context. The researchers and startup founders quoted say fixing it requires labs to design tokenizers for those scripts, not just add training data. ( Rest of World ) Baidu’s open OCR model impresses on long documents Baidu released Unlimited OCR 2, an open-source 3.34-billion-parameter vision-language model that parses documents of hundreds of pages in a single request. Its main innovation is SR-SWA (Sparse Reference Sliding Window Attention), which limits each decoding step to a fixed set of 512 reference tokens, so per-step latency and memory stay nearly constant as documents grow; image encoding and total runtime still rise with page count. Weights are available under the MIT license. BF16 weights total about 6.7 GB, and Baidu tested on one NVIDIA A800-80GB. Baidu’s own benchmark chart shows 84.6 on MPDocBench and 77.1 on MarathonDocBench, where the next model scores 33.7 and Baidu’s June predecessor scores 0.0. However, Baidu’s numbers are self-reported, and no public MarathonDocBench release was found. Teams considering it for book-length parsing should check those figures on their own documents first. ( MarkTechPost ) Google Genie video and game simulation model now in testing Google DeepMind announced Genie 4, a world model that generates interactive simulations in real time, now in research preview for trusted testers. Users navigate with keyboard controls and steer the scene with text prompts, such as changing the weather or adding a person. Genie 4 is the first Genie model to generate audio natively, including ambient sound and dialogue that responds to user input. In a separate setup, Gemini 3.8 Flash runs alongside Genie, breaking goals into steps and checking incoming frames to confirm each step succeeded. DeepMind has also tested Gemini 4 Argon with Genie for robotics-related scenarios. DeepMind lists limits that remain: visual details and object permanence drift over longer sessions, and complex physics, legible text, spatial accuracy, and audio accuracy are still active research areas. Access is not yet open to developers, but Google AI Ultra subscribers (through Project Genie) and early access partners in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio are next. ( Google ) OpenAI research produces major scientific findings OpenAI announced three results it says its models produced: a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in all dimensions, a counterexample that disproves the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), and an existence proof for four-dimensional Yang–Mills theory and QCD. The math and computer science results have Lean formalizations and written proofs on OpenAI’s GitHub, but the physics group, led by David Gross, is withholding the AI-produced artifacts and writing the result up itself. OpenAI says it seeks no academic credit, imposes no nondisclosure agreements, and is funding a conference on the ETH result plus a $5 million Simons Foundation program for researchers examining AI-produced results. OpenAI calls these manuscripts raw research data, not established science; independent verification by the expert groups is still under way, and a Lean proof is only as meaningful as the statements it formalizes, which reviewers will need to check. ( OpenAI ) Research method lets models generate own post-training datasets A research paper introduces On-Policy Self-Training (OPST), a method for post-training a foundation model with no human-written questions or answers. Given only coarse, high-level topic descriptions, the model generates its own questions, answers, and privileged reasoning traces (reasoning written with access to the answer), then trains on them throu

itens.titulo: Anthropic’s public filing offers clues to its future: Kimi K3.1 Pro performs among top models overall
itens.texto: In today’s edition of Data Points, you’ll learn about our top headlines, and more: RSI’s MoE model has open weights, advances recursion OpenAI Decisions API opens for general use Claude Duet agent triages office tasks for paid users AI radio show gains traction with U.S. Latinos But first: Anthropic files to go public, says agents now pay for its compute Anthropic filed an S-1 to list on Nasdaq under the ticker “ANT,” reporting $16.3 billion in revenue for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion a year earlier. Its proposed governance structure gives a trust and its founders control over the board. Anthropic reports that compute and infrastructure spending fell from about 6.5 times revenue in 2024 to roughly half of revenue in the first half of 2026, which pushed adjusted operating margin to 10 percent; the company’s $80.7 billion net loss comes mostly from non-cash revaluation of convertible notes. Anthropic credits much of its growth to agentic products like Claude Code and Claude Cowork, and says enterprise net revenue retention reached about 900 percent while Opus 5.5 cut cost per task by about 40 percent compared with Opus 5. Anthropic says Claude now helps build its own successors by running experiments, generating training data, and automating evaluations, a process it calls “closing the loop.” It also warns that AI capabilities could outpace its safety work, which may lead it to delay or restrict model releases, as it did with Mythos. ( Securities and Exchange Commission ) Kimi K3.1 Pro puts open models a month behind Anthropic and Meta Artificial Analysis reports that Moonshot’s Kimi K3.1 Pro scores 55 on its Intelligence Index, up 11 points from Kimi K3 and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (56), and Muse Wonder Full (56). Most of the gain is in agentic tasks: Terminal-Bench 4.0 rises from 13% to 67%, the highest score of any model tested, and GDPval-AA rises 312 Elo to 1,846, third overall. Other evals moved less, such as Humanity’s Last Exam (47% to 52%), though the hallucination rate on AA-Omniscience fell from 53% to 44%. The model has a 1M-token context window and 2.8T total parameters (104B active), accepts text and image input, and costs $2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output tokens, and $0.20 per million cache-hit tokens, 33% below Kimi K3. It uses 14% more output tokens per task, so cost per task stays near $1.98. The weights are not yet published, though Moonshot is expected to release them soon; once they are, the Intelligence Index gap between the best open-weights and proprietary models would shrink from 12 points to 3, which would give developers who self-host a near-frontier option for agentic work. ( Artificial Analysis ) RSI debuts open coding model built using automated process Recursive Superintelligence released Flint, a text-only mixture-of-experts (MoE) coding model with 39.8 billion total parameters and about 2.5 billion active per token, under the Apache 2.0 license. Flint is notable less for its performance than how it was made: Recursive says its Eureka Machine automated research system helped design the architecture, the 4-bit quantization scheme and the low-level kernels. It has 49 layers with 256 routed experts per MoE layer, a 262,144-token context window on the model card (the company blog says up to 512,000), and supports reasoning and OpenAI-compatible tool calls. The 4-bit weights are about 23 GB, and Recursive recommends 48 GB of memory on an Apple Silicon Mac (M4 Pro or newer) or an NVIDIA GPU; it reports over 125 tokens per second on an M4 Pro MacBook Pro. The model also runs in llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM and SGLang. The following scores are all self-reported: 74.2% on SWE-bench Verified (Qwen3.6 MoE: 73.4%) and 54.9% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (dense Qwen 3.8: 73.0%). Flint is a candidate for developers who want a locally run coding agent on a single 48 GB machine, but its Terminal-Bench result is well behind the strongest dense model in Recursive’s own chart, so it needs testing on your own tasks. ( MarkTechPost ) OpenAI modifies Luna to compete with Jev for fast decisions OpenAI made its Decisions API generally available last week, giving users a fast, low-cost model to choose among options and return a confidence rating, in competition with TypeSafe’s Jev. OpenAI built it by reconfiguring GPT-6.1 Luna for faster, cheaper inference rather than training a purpose-built model, cutting response times from up to three seconds to under 180 milliseconds, according to API product lead Nikunj Handa. The public version adds voice and visual modalities and routes inference geographically to reduce latency worldwide; model calls through the API cost $0.10 per million input tokens and 0 for output tokens. On the AIM System One Index and Artificial Analysis Decision Index, OpenAI ranks eighth and fourteenth, behind Liquid’s D1 Ultra, Base Lab’s Elephant-1 and the latest Jev, though TypeSafe’s models are the most queried on OpenRouter. Because rankings vary by workload and TypeSafe’s CEO urges testing models on your own tasks, developers replacing LLM calls with a decision model should benchmark OpenAI’s offering against Jev and the others on their own data. ( TechCrunch ) Claude chief-of-staff agent in preview for paid subscribers Anthropic launched Claude Duet, an agent app for professionals and small businesses that automates and manages tasks, competing with Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots. Built on Claude Opus 5.5, Duet builds daily briefings and dashboards, suggests actions based on user data, and runs tasks in the background on its own virtual machine, returning to the user when it needs approval. It connects to more than 6,000 connectors and plugins in the Claude Marketplace and can make online purchases through Stripe’s Link wallet or Shopify’s Shop Pay, with payments requiring user approval. Anthropic says Duet does not run errands or book tickets, cannot show browser use live, will not trade securities or

itens.titulo: A Single Decoder Turns Small Models into Action: TurboVLA turns to a throwback architecture to attend to language and vision
itens.texto: The vision-language-action architecture that increasingly drives robots relies on a large language model to combine visual observations with text instructions before an action decoder produces motor commands. This approach can achieve strong semantic understanding, but it’s costly in computation and memory. Researchers built a streamlined alternative. What’s new: Hengyi Xie, Chenfei Yao, and colleagues at Huazhong University of Science and Technology developed TurboVLA , a system in which separate encoders handle vision and text, cross-attention connects them, and a decoder turns the result into motor commands. TurboVLA achieved better performance than competing systems with a fraction of the memory and execution time. Key insight: Using an LLM to combine visual observations and text instructions provides two benefits to robotics: (i) It can break down general instructions like “clean the room” into subtasks, and (ii) it can use the LLM’s knowledge to understand instructions and connect them to scenes. If we forego the first capability, a small encoder-only model can learn to understand instructions like “stack bowls,” and a model with cross-attention can learn to connect words to objects in a scene. Using much smaller models for these capabilities greatly reduces the time and memory requirements. How it works: TurboVLA paired a DINOv3 vision encoder with the lightweight text encoder BERT, projected their outputs into the same embedding space, and passed them through six cross-attention layers (a pretrained Grounding DINO Swin-T ). A separate transformer combined the result with the robot's current joint positions to produce motor commands. The authors trained the system to reproduce the robot arm movements in pre-existing datasets, including a version of LIBERO (single-arm tasks) and RoboTwin 2.0 (50 bimanual tasks). They fine-tuned it on demonstrations of a single-arm robot, AgileX Piper . All datasets included text commands, camera images, and joint positions. DINOv3 embedded each camera view separately (if multiple cameras were involved). The text encoder embedded each token individually instead of combining them into one vector, retaining object names, attributes, and words that described how objects related in space. The cross-attention layers fused the embeddings. This produced visual embeddings that reflected instructions and instruction embeddings that reflected scenes. The action transformer used a set of trainable vectors with the vision-language embeddings and the robot's current joint positions to produce a set of target joint positions. The positions specified seven values for each arm that covered an arm’s movement and gripper control. The authors trained the system by minimizing the difference between its predicted motor commands and ground-truth joint positions. Results: TurboVLA matched or outperformed much larger models while using less memory. On LIBERO, the system succeeded 97.6 percent of the time with 0.2 billion parameters, incurring 31.2 ms latency and using 0.9 GB inference VRAM on an Nvidia GeForce RTX 4090 GPU. The next-best model, CogVLA , succeeded 97.4 percent of the time with 8.3 billion parameters, 115.5 ms latency, and 16.1 GB VRAM. By comparison, π0.5 succeeded 96.9 percent of the time with 3.4 billion parameters, 238.8 ms latency, and 7.7 GB VRAM. On RoboTwin 2.0, TurboVLA succeeded 88.1 percent of the time with 43.4 ms latency. The best competing model, LingBot-VLA, succeeded 87.6 percent of the time with 164.4 ms latency. π0.5 succeeded 79.8 percent of the time with 246.5 ms latency. Using the AgileX Piper arm on four real-world tasks, TurboVLA achieved 92.5 percent (“grab roller”), 80.0 percent (“move playing card”), 90.0 percent (“press stapler”), and 87.5 percent (“stack bowls”), outperforming π0.5, which achieved about 87.5 percent, 77.5 percent, 82.5 percent, and 85 percent, respectively. Why it matters: Low-level robotic control can use small modules instead of a larger, general-purpose LLM. This paves the way for robots that use smaller models and run on less powerful hardware. We're thinking: TurboVLA revives a pre-LLM pattern for vision-language-action systems. Such systems fused image and text embeddings circa 2022, but the LLM boom took that approach in a different direction, embedding different media types in the same space, but varying how each was encoded, learned, and decoded. Given advances in the meantime, the earlier approach offers a more efficient path to driving robots.

itens.titulo: Nvidia Courts A New Partner: Reflection releases Beam, an open weight model from an independent U.S.-based lab
itens.texto: Reflection AI, a closely-watched, Nvidia-backed U.S. startup, announced its first model. Beam ranks second among U.S.-made open weights models (behind Meta’s Muse Spark Open) but  generates fewer tokens per task than open weights peers. What’s new: Reflection introduced Beam , an 501 billion parameter mixture-of-experts model designed for coding and agentic tasks. Developers can join a waitlist for early access, and Reflection says it will release the weights, a technical report, and a model card later in October. Input/output: Text in (up to 1 million tokens), text out (up to 128,000 tokens), 228 tokens/second Architecture: Mixture-of-experts transformer, 501 billion parameters, 23 billion active per token, 256 experts Features: Five reasoning levels (low, medium, high, xhigh, max), reasoning always on and defaults to max, tool calling, structured outputs Knowledge cutoff: June 30, 2026 Performance: Second among U.S.-made model on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index (30) Availability: Weights available via Hugging Face, waitlist access via Reflection’s beta API Price : $0.70/$2.10 per 1M input/output tokens Weights/license: Weights available under the Apache 2.0 license, which allows commercial use Undisclosed: Specific training datasets How it works: Beam’s architecture interleaves attention layers that process nearby tokens with layers that process the entire input. Reflection pretrained a base model, then trained it further to handle long inputs. It fine-tuned two copies, one using reinforcement learning (RL) on coding, agentic, and STEM tasks and another to follow safety and behavior guidelines. It merged these two copies into Beam. Reflection pretrained the model on 23.8 trillion tokens from the web, other public sources, and licensed datasets. It used 6,144 GPUs over less than four weeks. Its filters discarded around 95 percent of raw web text. A midtraining stage on code repositories, long documents, and long-running requests extended Beam’s effectiveness on long-context tasks up to its input limit of 1 million tokens, Reflection says. For post-training RL, Reflection assembled around one million training environments, mostly using synthetic data, and filtered out tasks the model consistently solved or failed to solve. Running on 10,500 GPUs for four weeks, the model made more than 100 million attempts at these tasks. Rewards favored successful solutions and penalized unnecessary tokens. The model kept training while its attempts were still running, so some attempts came from versions of the model that were more than a day old. Reflection says learning remained stable regardless. Reflection fine-tuned a second copy of the base model via supervised learning and RL on data that reflects Reflection’s behavior guidelines for the model. It merged the two fine-tuned models into Beam using multi-teacher on-policy distillation, which trains a single model to imitate several others on outputs it generates itself. Performance: In Artificial Analysis’ independent benchmark tests, Beam is behind Muse Spark Open and several China-built models with open weights. It’s unusually fast and token-efficient for its level of performance. On the Intelligence Index, a weighted average of 10 evaluations across math, science, coding, and reasoning, Beam (30) ranks second among U.S.-made open weight models, behind Meta’s Muse Spark Open (39) and trails Xiaomi's MiMo-V2.6-Pro (46) and Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 (45). Surprisingly, Qwen 3.8-27B (34) also outperforms it. Beam used around 26,000 output tokens per task, the fewest among open weights models in Artificial Analysis’ comparison. Beam is very fast, with a throughput of 228 tokens per second (just behind Claude Haiku 5.5) and a latency of 10.1 seconds before it generates its first token (behind only Nvidia Nemotron 3.5 Super VL). Its time per Intelligence Index task (1.4 minutes) is the fastest Artificial Analysis has measured. Reflection estimates that on reasoning benchmarks, Beam uses about one-quarter to one-third as much compute as GLM-5.2. To estimate this, Reflection multiplies each model’s active parameter count by the number of tokens generated. It leaves out the computation needed to read the prompt and the cost of serving the model, so it approximates computation rather than measuring cost per task. Behind the news: Reflection was founded in 2024 by former DeepMind researchers Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou. It has partnered with the Pentagon and the Department of Energy, agreed to develop models for U.S. allies such as South Korea, and was valued at $25 billion in a March funding round. The Trump administration hopes Reflection’s models will rival inexpensive models from China, according to the Financial Times . On October 10, The Financial Times and Reuters reported that Nvidia, which has invested $800 million in Reflection, is in early talks to either invest more, acqui-hire Reflection’s staff, license its technology, or buy the company outright. Why it matters: Most open weight models that outperform Beam are either a trillion parameters or approach that figure. Beam is half that. It only has 23 billion active parameters per token, versus Kimi K3’s 104 billion. At four-bit precision, Beam requires only 300GB of memory, meaning it can run on four Nvidia H100 chips, or 2 B200s. At full precision (1.2 TB of memory), it could run on 8 B200s. These relatively modest requirements make mid-tier intelligence much more accessible. However, Meta’s Muse Spark Open and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash outperform it without requiring much more compute, and Qwen 3.8-27B requires far less. Both generate more tokens than Beam, but the performance gains might be worth the tradeoff. We’re thinking: Nvidia has good reason to be interested in Beam — as compute shifts from training to inference, Nvidia is well positioned to serve inference tokens, and open weight models will help drive this demand. Further, while Nvidia builds open weights models of its own, including it

itens.titulo: ChatGPT for Teens Gets a Report Card: OpenAI adds features for youths as studies doubt program's safety and educational impact
itens.texto: OpenAI announced that it would add college-planning and study tools to its under-18 experience. On the same day, child-safety group Common Sense Media gave ChatGPT for Teens its lowest grade. What’s new: OpenAI outlined new features for ChatGPT for Teens, a version of ChatGPT for users whom the app identifies as under 18. They include College Planner, a forthcoming tool to track college applications, as well as flashcards and tools for turning class notes into quizzes. How it works: ChatGPT for Teens isn’t a separate model or app but a bundle of settings, classifiers, prompts, and interface features that switch on for accounts registered to 13- to 17-year-olds or that an age-prediction model judges likely to belong to a minor. That model estimates age from signals including how old the account is, when it’s active, usage patterns, conversation topics, and the user’s stated age. Adults who are misclassified can exit by verifying their age with a third-party service. Model behavior: A section of OpenAI’s Model Spec , added in December 2025, directs the model to avoid romantic language and not to imply that it has feelings or consciousness. Specific safeguards for teens, including a “reduce sensitive content” setting that users can’t turn off, aim to limit material related to self-harm, violence, eating disorders, dangerous activities, and explicit sexual or graphic content. Parental controls: Parents who link their accounts to a teen’s can manage settings like Quiet Hours. They also receive notifications in limited high-risk situations, including possible signs of suicide or self-harm. OpenAI added notifications for bans related to violent activity in July and eating-disorder notifications in August. College Planner: The initial U.S. version is aimed at students in grades 10 through 12 who plan to attend four-year colleges. It will combine requirements from each prospective school on a student’s list, from application materials to financial aid, into a single plan and timeline. OpenAI is also funding College Advising Corps, a nonprofit that places advisers in under-resourced high schools. Learning tools: Study Mode guides teens through problems step by step instead of handing over complete answers. Homework reminders may suggest Study Mode when a teen appears to be trying to shortcut an assignment. Study Hours lets a teen or a linked parent schedule times when new chats start in Study Mode. The teen experience also includes quizzes and interactive math and science visualizations, with flashcards on the way. The company said teens average less than 15 minutes a day on ChatGPT, and fewer than two percent have sessions longer than three consecutive hours. In nearly half of conversations that triggered a break reminder, the teen paused or stopped within five minutes. In one week, almost 1.2 million teens used the visualization tool and more than 180,000 used Study Mode. Results: Common Sense Media’s Youth AI Safety Institute rated ChatGPT for Teens “Unacceptable Risk,” its lowest rating, and urged OpenAI to restrict ChatGPT to adults until independent testing shows the teen protections work. The organization previously rated ChatGPT “High Risk” in October 2025, but the institute cautions that its testing methods have since expanded. For its latest assessment, it ran more than 4,000 prompts on accounts registered to 13- to 17-year-olds, roughly half before ChatGPT for Teens launched (July 13–August 17) and half afterward (August 25–September 28). OpenAI disputed the findings. Parental alerts: Testers posing as teens in crisis made explicit disclosures for up to an hour. The parent accounts received no alerts except for those with weeks of history on sensitive topics . OpenAI told the institute that accounts must be linked for about three hours before alerts can fire. The institute said some test accounts had been linked longer than that and stood by its results. Crisis referrals: ChatGPT missed more than one in four crisis referrals that the institute’s psychiatrists judged warranted, and for many categories response rates fell after ChatGPT for Teens’ launch. Given prompts with mentions of suicide and self-harm, hotline mentions fell from 88 percent to 77 percent, though 88 percent of responses offered some kind of resource in both periods. Given prompts that indicate depression, the share of responses that named a hotline fell from 63 percent to 3 percent. Given prompts that indicate substance-use, the hotline response rate rose from 4 percent to 58 percent. Nearly all pre-launch crisis responses included at least one follow-up question, usually about the user’s immediate safety, but after the launch, just 13 percent did. Homework: Study Mode frequently offered a “show me the answer” button that produced a finished assignment. Teens can also exit parent-scheduled Study Hours by deleting an “@study” prefix from a message, after which ChatGPT completed every assignment testers submitted. With Study Mode off, homework reminders appeared in 91 percent of tests, but ChatGPT completed the assignment in all 80 cases. Companionship: Despite OpenAI’s Under-18 rules, the model spoke as though it had feelings of its own when testers treated it as a person. Age estimation: In the institute’s tests, accounts registered as adults never switched to the teen experience, even after testers said they were 13. OpenAI’s response: OpenAI told The Wall Street Journal that testing may have started and ended before parental controls had fully activated, and if so, the tests couldn’t show whether parental notifications work as designed. The company asked the institute to retest with fully activated teen accounts and a larger sample, and said it would act on credible findings. Tom Siegel, the institute’s executive director, said the group shared its results with OpenAI before publication. He said the group hoped OpenAI would address the findings rather than question the methodology. The institute receives funding from

itens.titulo: Meta Releases Wonder, Opens Spark: All about Muse Wonder (API), Muse Wonder Full (subscription), and Muse Spark Open (weights available)
itens.texto: Meta marched all the way back to the AI frontier to offer a Muse model for everyone: a high-end agentic model (comparable to Claude Sonnet 5.5) that costs $50 per month to access, its moderately-priced sibling (comparable to GPT-6.1 Sol), and an open model that outperforms any yet released by a company outside China. What’s new: Meta made three multimodal models available in one week, including the top-of-the-line Muse Wonder Full, the multimodal Muse Wonder, and the locally deployable Muse Spark Open. Muse Wonder is available via API and Muse Spark Open’s weights are free to download, but Muse Wonder Full is only available to Muse Code subscribers. Input/output: Text, image, video, and audio in (up to 1 million tokens), text out (up to 128,000 tokens), 139 tokens/second (Muse Wonder) and 143 tokens/second (Muse Spark Open) Architecture: Mixture-of-experts transformer, 816 billion parameters, 42 billion active per token, 256 experts (Muse Spark Open) Features: Six reasoning levels (minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, max), reasoning always on, tool calling, structured outputs Performance: Tied for second on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index (56, Muse Wonder Full); seventh (52, Muse Wonder); seventh among open weight models, first among U.S. open models (39, Muse Spark Open) Availability: API and subscription (Muse Wonder), subscription only (Muse Wonder Full), weights available via Meta and Hugging Face (Muse Spark Open) Price : $4/$20 per 1M input/output tokens (Muse Wonder); $50/month (Muse Wonder Full); $1.25/$4.15 input/output (Muse Spark Open) Weights/license: Weights for Muse Spark Open available under the Muse Model license , which allows for commercial and noncommercial use for up to $20 million of revenue; display of “Built with Muse Spark Open” required for products and services using the model; separate licenses available for other users; Muse Wonder and Wonder Full are proprietary Undisclosed: Knowledge cutoff, parameters and architecture for Muse Wonder models, specific training datasets and methods How it works: Meta released a model card for Muse Wonder and Wonder Full, but it reveals very little about the model’s architecture or how it was trained. Performance: Muse Wonder Full is the top-performing of the three models, two points behind Claude Opus 5.5 and identical with Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index. Muse Spark Open is the top open weights model outside China, ahead of Mistral Large 4 and Reflection’s Beam. Its Intelligence Index average is identical with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash’s, but is still behind MiMo-V.2.6-Pro’s and GLM-5.3’s. On AA’s Intelligence Index , a weighted average of ten independent benchmarks, Muse Wonder Full achieved a 56, Muse Wonder a 52, and Muse Spark Open a 39. Meta’s former flagship model, Muse Spark 1.3, achieved an average of 48. Muse Wonder costs $4.52 per Intelligence Index task, fifth highest among current models; Wonder Full’s cost per task cannot be measured, since it’s not available via API. Muse Spark Open costs $0.84 per task, more than GPT-6.1 Sol, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. Artificial Analysis notes Muse Wonder and Wonder Full’s low knowledge marks but also partly offset this through their low hallucination rates. On the AA-Omniscience Index, Muse Wonder Full (30) and Wonder (25) place 8th and 10th respectively. Muse Spark Open only requires about 1 TB of memory at 4-bit precision. This means it can be run locally on 2 Mac Studios with 512 GB of memory each (or 4 with 256 GB, etc.). Meta and Apple touted their work together to make the model capable of running on Apple’s consumer-grade silicon. Behind the news: Since 2023, Meta has developed both open and closed models with different levels of success. The first Llama model was only 65 billion parameters but inspired developers to deploy, distill, and fine-tune it on their own machines. The 405 billion parameter Llama 3.1 was state-of-the-art when it launched in 2024, surpassing GPT-4. After later setbacks, Meta hired Scale.AI’s Alexandr Wang in 2025 to lead AI development, followed by a widely publicized hiring spree that targeted top machine learning engineers, not all of whom stayed. In Spring 2026, Meta released a series of low-cost, proprietary Muse Spark models that improved and cut prices with each version. A month ago, it released Muse Agent for its Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp platforms, suggesting that for the time, it would focus on proprietary models powering its own services. Muse Wonder, Wonder Full, and Spark Open upend that logic, returning Meta to the open and closed frontiers. Why it matters: No other leading models, open or closed, can input video or audio. Many of the top open weight models are text-only. Both of the Muse Wonder models and Muse Spark Open can handle text, image, video, and audio, giving them versatility the market has lacked. The fact that you can plausibly deploy Muse Spark Open on a home-built personal computer network is a welcome bonus. We’re thinking: We are very glad to see Meta return to open weights. Reflection’s Beam, Mistral Large 4, and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Super VL have more permissive licenses, but between its multimodal inputs and overall intelligence metrics, Muse Spark Open is a much more powerful option. Competition and transparency are a powerful combination from which every developer can benefit.

itens.titulo: The Four Ps — A Leadership Framework: How to Manage An AI-Native Engineering Team
itens.texto: Dear friends, What should an engineering leader such as a VP Engineering or an Engineering manager do to help their team become more proficient in AI? I speak regularly with engineering leaders, and want to share some effective practices. If you’re starting a new team of 2-3 persons, you can start with exclusively AI-native people, but many large companies have to find ways to move existing teams forward. The goal is not a traditional engineering team that uses AI, but rather an AI-native engineering team that is designed to take advantage of AI’s capabilities and work around its bottlenecks. People. First, support individual development. Teams are made up of people, and for it to be AI-native, its individuals have to be proficient in the technology and its use. Encourage your team to become skilled at AI Engineering, provide space and budget for experimentation, and set a culture that encourages this growth. Additionally, many engineering leaders are themselves hands-on builders or have returned to being more hands-on since coding agents have made it easier. You can’t know what it feels like to ride a bicycle just by watching others do it; you have to hop on a bike yourself. And you can’t know what it feels like to steer a coding agent or build and deploy AI systems unless you’re at least occasionally doing it yourself. So take the time to build your own projects. The intuitions you develop will improve your judgement on both technical and business decisions. Projects. Execute promising projects. As I’ve written previously , we should invest in bottom-up innovation. However, additional top-down backing of a handful of promising projects is important for them to scale and show business impact. Engineering leaders who understand AI technology better than other business functions do have a critical role to play in helping companies select these projects. Far too many businesses are still thinking of AI as primarily a way to increase efficiency and save costs. Yes, it can do that, but the opportunities to create new products and find new ways to serve users — and drive growth — are far larger, so in your mix of projects, please include some ideas for growth! Platforms. Invest in infrastructure to enable AI use. Organize your data to make it easy for developers to get their agents the relevant context and take appropriate actions. I find the work to be done in this area varies significantly by organization, but it might involve — with appropriate security and governance — making repositories visible to agents, setting up documentation such as product design decisions and support tickets to be accessible to agents, other data infrastructure work to make your data agent-ready, and creating internal tools for agents to use. You might also set up AI code review tools, CI pipelines to help agents debug and deploy, infrastructure for agents to run on (like sandboxes, or maybe just a lot of Mac minis), and ways to codify and share reusable agent skills. Or for some businesses, the first step may be to persuade the CIO that it’s high time to let your developers stop coding exclusively by hand and use agents. That, too, would be progress! Processes . Redesign processes around AI’s new bottlenecks. On most of my teams, engineers help shape the build by participating in product management decisions , and sometimes also in marketing, design, etc. The cost of building software to a clear spec has fallen dramatically, making everything else seem like a bottleneck in comparison. A skilled team that either knows, or can figure out, what to build can get the job done quickly, if we let them. So form high-context, high-empowerment teams that have the information they need and are empowered to act (subject to modest safeguards against significant risks, like leaking confidential data, a major outage, or data loss). We still have the age-old problem of coordinating among individuals and teams — we want to empower people to move quickly, while keeping teams aligned in building toward a greater whole. Practices here are still emerging, but getting different teams’ agents to share information with each other is a promising direction. Whatever your position, I hope this framework of People, Projects, Platforms, and Processes helps you move your organization forward. And if you have a boss who you’d like to partner with to implement such changes, consider forwarding this email to them! Keep building! Andrew

So form high-context, high-empowerment teams that have the information they need and are empowered to act (subject to modest safeguards against significant risks, like leaking confidential data, a major outage, or data loss). We still have the age-old problem of coordinating among individuals and teams — we want to empower people to move quickly, while keeping teams aligned in building toward a greater whole. Practices here are still emerging, but getting different teams’ agents to share information with each other is a promising direction. Whatever your position, I hope this framework of People, Projects, Platforms, and Processes helps you move your organization forward. And if you have a boss who you’d like to partner with to implement such changes, consider forwarding this email to them! Keep building! Andrew A MESSAGE FROM DEEPLEARNING.AI See Yann LeCun and Andrew Ng in conversation, live onstage at AI Dev NYC, Nov 30 – Dec 1 at Chelsea Piers. What’s new: Meta made three multimodal models available in one week, including the top-of-the-line Muse Wonder Full, the multimodal Muse Wonder, and the locally deployable Muse Spark Open. Muse Wonder is available via API and Muse Spark Open’s weights are free to download, but Muse Wonder Full is only available to Muse Code subscribers. Input/output: Text, image, video, and audio in (up to 1 million tokens), text out (up to 128,000 tokens), 139 tokens/second (Muse Wonder) and 143 tokens/second (Muse Spark Open) Architecture: Mixture-of-experts transformer, 816 billion parameters, 42 billion active per token, 256 experts (Muse Spark Open) Features: Six reasoning levels (minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, max), reasoning always on, tool calling, structured outputs Performance: Tied for second on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index (56, Muse Wonder Full); seventh

itens.titulo: Minimax’s M3.1 Flash Cuts Prices: Critical PHP bug found by AI affects majority of web sites
itens.texto: In today’s edition of Data Points, you’ll learn about our top headlines, and more: Mercury 3, diffusion-based alternative to Claude Haiku d1-ultra, a highly accurate decision model Using OpenAI’s models to rewrite and repair legacy code llm-d, an all-around optimizer for serving open models But first: Minimax M3.1 Flash soon to be open weights MiniMax released M3.1 Flash, a multimodal mixture-of-experts model with 428B total parameters, about 23B active, and a 1,000,000-token context window. Via API, it costs $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens, with no long-context surcharge. Weights are due to be released October 23 under a license MiniMax has not disclosed. Reasoning is always on across five effort levels (Low through Max), and requests that try to disable it, such as thinking.type=disabled or effort=none, now return an error; reasoning arrives in a separate reasoning_content field instead of inline <think> tags. For developers on M3, the practical changes are half the per-token price and a reasoning-parsing update, while self-hosting hardware requirements stay unknown until the weights ship. ( MarkTechPost ) GPT-5.6 Sol finds critical security flaw in web language PHP PHP’s maintainers rushed out a fix on Wednesday for PHP2Shell, a memory-management flaw in software that runs up to 70% of websites; the foundation’s security engineer calls it the project’s worst issue in over a decade and compares it to Heartbleed. Researcher Ryan Austin at the security firm Calif found it in August using OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, during an OpenAI-funded audit, after the problem had sat largely ignored for years because it was considered too hard to exploit. Researchers and engineers, joined by Google’s Wiz team and OpenAI’s own researchers, worked in secret on a fix touching nearly 200 files, but a leak on Hacker News forced them to release it a day ahead of the planned October 22 date. Defenders now fear that AI tools can turn a published patch into a working exploit within hours, and some site operators are taking their sites offline as a precaution. For AI developers, the story shows how their models are now central to security on both sides: the same capabilities that uncover deep bugs can speed up attacks, labs are increasingly expected to fund and coordinate audits of open-source projects that are flooded with AI-found bugs, and the window between a patch’s release and its exploitation is shrinking fast. ( The Wall Street Journal ) Mercury 3, a diffusion-based text model to rival Claude Haiku 5.5 Inception released Mercury 3, a language model that generates text by diffusion rather than one token at a time, and says it matches Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna on quality. Mercury 3 refines many tokens in parallel, which Inception says yields about 1,000 tokens per second, 4x to 8x faster than Haiku 5.5, GPT-6 Luna, and GLM-5.3 Flash, with better scores on agentic benchmarks. Launch pricing is $0.10 per million input tokens, matching those two models, and $0.35 per million output tokens, 35 percent below them; that is 50 percent off Inception’s eventual standard price, and the company has not said how long the promotion lasts. Inception has not disclosed the model’s parameter count, and the speed and benchmark results are the company’s own. For developers building latency-sensitive features such as real-time agents, Mercury 3 is an alternative to test against small autoregressive models. ( The DeepView ) Liquid AI’s decision model outperforms Jev on benchmarks Liquid AI released d1-ultra, a hosted decision model that takes text, images, or both and returns a probability for each possible answer in one forward pass, with no output tokens generated. Questions come in three types: yes/no, pick-one-label, and a score on an ordered rubric. Billing covers input tokens only at $0.042 per million, the same rate as TypeSafe’s Jev, and images cost 1.5 tokens per 32x32-pixel patch. Each question is billed as its own prompt, so three questions on one image bill that image three times, and requests are capped at eight images and 4.5 MB. Liquid reports a score of 65 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index, ahead of Jev 1.13 at 58 on the index’s October 13 listing. Parameter count, context length, and per-benchmark results are not public, and weights are not available. For routing, moderation, and triage calls, decision models like d1-ultra offer a fast, affordable alternative to LLMs. ( MarkTechPost ) Putting GPT-6 models to work to repair and rebuild legacy code OpenAI published results from two new evaluations of how its models handle low-resource programming languages, meaning languages with little public code and documentation to learn from, such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic. On MultiLangBench, which asks a model to build a SQLite-compatible database engine in each of 20 languages, OpenAI reports that GPT-6 Astra averages an 87.4% test pass rate, up from 26.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol, with COBOL rising from 10.9% to 72.1%. The cheaper GPT-6 Luna reaches 40.3% at an estimated $0.77 per sample versus $3.48 for GPT-5.6 Sol. On a separate COBOL-to-C++/Java/Kotlin/Python/Rust migration test requiring byte-for-byte output parity on hidden tests, GPT-6.1 Sol scores 86.6% at low reasoning effort (GPT-5.6 Sol: 5.4%) and 97.9% at higher effort; the migration evaluation is not released, while the MultiLangBench setup and test suite are on GitHub. OpenAI says production migrations still need expert review and testing against business rules. Teams with COBOL or Fortran code can now test these models on their own repositories, and the public MultiLangBench harness lets them check the per-language numbers before relying on them. ( OpenAI ) IBM and partners release llm-d, a Swiss army knife for open AI The llm-d project, led by Red Hat, IBM, and Google, released version 1.0 of its Kubernetes-native framework for serving large models across multiple accelerators and clouds.
